content: Acute asthma exacerbations are a common reason for emergency department (ED) visits, with approximately 12-16% of patients experiencing a relapse that requires further medical intervention within two weeks of discharge. The management of acute asthma focuses on rapidly reversing bronchospasm and reducing airway inflammation. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of corticosteroids—administered orally, intramuscularly, or intravenously—in preventing relapse in patients discharged from an acute care setting, such as the ED, after treatment for an acute asthma exacerbation. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register and reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. They also contacted study authors to identify unpublished data. The most recent search was completed in October 2006. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials comparing corticosteroids (oral, intramuscular, or inhaled) with placebo for outpatient treatment of asthma exacerbations in both adults and children. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Authors of the included studies were contacted for additional information. Ultimately, six trials involving 374 participants were included in the analysis. One study investigated intramuscular corticosteroids, while the remaining five focused on oral corticosteroids. Although no new placebo-controlled trials were identified in the latest search, an additional study on intramuscular corticosteroids was included. The results demonstrated that significantly fewer patients in the corticosteroid group experienced a relapse requiring additional care within the first week after discharge (Relative Risk [RR] 0.38; 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.2 to 0.74). This beneficial effect persisted over the first 21 days (RR 0.47; 95% CI 0.25 to 0.89). Additionally, patients treated with corticosteroids had a lower likelihood of subsequent hospitalization (RR 0.35; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.95). Corticosteroid use also reduced the need for short-acting beta2-agonists, with patients requiring fewer activations per day (Mean Difference [MD] -3.3 activations/day; 95% CI -5.6 to -1.0). Pulmonary function test results (Standardized Mean Difference [SMD] 0.045; 95% CI -0.47 to 0.56) and reported side effects (SMD 0.03; 95% CI -0.38 to 0.44) showed no significant differences between the corticosteroid and placebo groups during the first 7 to 10 days. However, there was statistically significant heterogeneity in the side effect data, while all other outcomes were consistent across studies. The analysis indicated that treating as few as ten patients with corticosteroids could prevent one relapse requiring additional care after an asthma exacerbation. In conclusion, a short course of corticosteroids following an acute asthma exacerbation significantly reduces the risk of relapse, hospitalizations, and the need for short-acting beta2-agonists, without a notable increase in side effects. Both intramuscular and oral corticosteroids were found to be effective in achieving these outcomes.
